Dr. Lena Okafor Principal Environmental Scientist Connecticut Licensed Environmental Professional No. LEP-2241 Halcyon Environmental Consultants Inc.

Date: May 2, 2025

\ 

This document is an executive summary of the full Phase II Environmental Site Assessment report. The complete report with all appendices --- including laboratory analytical data, boring logs, figures, and photographs --- is available under separate cover as Halcyon Project No. HEC-2025-0412.

**[1. Introduction and Purpose]{.underline}**

This Phase II Environmental Site Assessment (\"Phase II ESA\" or \"Assessment\") was performed by Halcyon Environmental Consultants Inc. (\"Halcyon\") at the request of Meridian Gateway Holdings LLC (\"Client\") in connection with the Client\'s proposed acquisition of a long-term ground lease for the property located at 10-30 Pier Street, Port Calloway, Connecticut 06801 (Assessor\'s Parcel No. 127-003-0045) (the \"Subject Property\" or \"Property\") from the City of Port Calloway Redevelopment Authority (the \"Authority\"). The Client intends to develop the Subject Property as a mixed-use waterfront project consisting of a residential tower with ground-floor commercial and retail space, subject to the terms of the proposed ground lease.

This Phase II ESA was conducted to further evaluate recognized environmental conditions (\"RECs\") identified in the Phase I Environmental Site Assessment previously prepared by Halcyon for the Client (Report No. HEC-2025-0318, dated March 15, 2025) (the \"Phase I ESA\"). The Phase I ESA identified RECs related to the Subject Property\'s historical use as a ship repair and dry dock facility from approximately 1942 through 1987. Specifically, the Phase I ESA identified potential petroleum hydrocarbon contamination associated with former underground storage tank (\"UST\") operations in the northwest corner of the Property, as well as potential contamination within the filled former dry dock basin in the southeastern portion of the Property.

The purpose of this Phase II investigation is to determine the nature, extent, and concentrations of potential soil and groundwater contamination at the Subject Property, to evaluate the existing Environmental Land Use Restriction (\"ELUR\") recorded against the Property, and to provide preliminary remediation cost estimates to inform the Client\'s due diligence evaluation and the proposed lease transaction. The data and findings presented herein are intended to assist the Client and the Client\'s advisors in assessing environmental risk, estimating remediation liabilities, and structuring the terms of the proposed ground lease accordingly.

This Assessment was performed in general conformance with ASTM Standard E1903-19, *Standard Practice for Environmental Site Assessments: Phase II Environmental Site Assessment Process*, and applicable Connecticut Department of Energy and Environmental Protection (\"CT DEEP\") guidance documents, including the CT DEEP *Remediation Standard Regulations* (\"RSRs\"), Conn. Agencies Regs. § 22a-133k-1 *et seq.*, and CT DEEP\'s *Guidance for Conducting Phase II Environmental Site Assessments* (revised 2021).

At the Client\'s direction, copies of this report are being provided to the Client\'s legal counsel, Hargrove & Linden LLP (Attention: Rebecca Tsang, Esq.), and to the Client\'s construction lender, Bayside Federal Lending Corp. (Attention: Sandra Milliken, Senior Vice President, Environmental Risk). Third-party reliance on this report is subject to the limitations set forth in Section 8 herein.

**[2. Property Description and Site Background]{.underline}**

**2.1 Property Description**

The Subject Property is located at 10-30 Pier Street, Port Calloway, Connecticut 06801, and is identified in the Port Calloway Assessor\'s records as Parcel No. 127-003-0045. The Property comprises approximately 3.2 acres (139,392 square feet) of land situated along the Long Island Sound waterfront in Port Calloway\'s designated Waterfront Revitalization District.

The current fee simple owner of the Subject Property is the City of Port Calloway Redevelopment Authority, with principal offices at 75 Municipal Plaza, Port Calloway, CT 06801. The Authority acquired the Property through eminent domain proceedings concluded in 2012 as part of its broader waterfront revitalization initiative.

The Property is currently vacant. All former structures associated with the historical ship repair and dry dock operations have been demolished, and the site has been graded and partially capped with compacted fill material. The parcel includes approximately 480 linear feet of bulkhead along the Long Island Sound waterfront on the eastern boundary. The bulkhead is of reinforced concrete and timber construction and, based on Halcyon\'s visual observations during the field investigation, is in fair to poor condition.

The boundaries of the Subject Property are as follows:

> • **North:** Pier Street (public roadway)
>
> • **East:** Long Island Sound waterfront promenade, subject to a 15-foot public pedestrian access easement recorded at Volume 395, Page 112 of the Port Calloway Land Records
>
> • **South:** Parcel 127-003-0044, a parcel retained by the Authority for future public park development
>
> • **West:** Harbor Avenue (public roadway)

A 20-foot-wide public utility easement for underground electric and sewer infrastructure runs along the northern boundary of the Property (Pier Street frontage), as recorded at Volume 388, Page 201 of the Port Calloway Land Records. The Subject Property is zoned WRD-3 (Mixed-Use High Density) within the Port Calloway Waterfront Revitalization District (\"WRD\"), which permits residential, commercial, retail, and mixed-use development, subject to applicable environmental restrictions and land use approvals.

**2.2 Historical Use and Site Background**

Based on historical records reviewed during the Phase I ESA --- including Sanborn fire insurance maps, city directory listings, building department records, aerial photographs, and CT DEEP file reviews --- the Subject Property was operated as a ship repair and dry dock facility from approximately 1942 to 1987. The facility was originally constructed during World War II to support naval vessel maintenance and was subsequently operated as a commercial ship repair yard by several private operators through the late 1980s. Operations at the facility historically included vessel hull maintenance and repair, marine engine overhaul, painting and surface coating, marine fueling operations, and solvent degreasing of metal components.

Historical records indicate that underground storage tanks for diesel fuel and waste oil were formerly located in the northwest portion of the Property. Records from the Port Calloway Fire Marshal\'s office and CT DEEP UST registration files suggest that at least two USTs --- a 10,000-gallon diesel fuel tank and a 5,000-gallon waste oil tank --- were installed in the 1950s and removed by the prior facility operator in approximately 1988. However, closure documentation for these USTs is incomplete: the available records do not include confirmation soil sampling results or evidence of a formal UST closure report filed with CT DEEP, and the status of these tanks in the CT DEEP Leaking Underground Storage Tank (\"LUST\") database is listed as \"closure pending/incomplete.\"

A dry dock basin was located in the southeastern portion of the Property. The dry dock, which measured approximately 120 feet in length and 40 feet in width, was decommissioned when the ship repair facility ceased operations. During site demolition activities conducted in approximately 2013--2014 under the Authority\'s direction, the dry dock basin was filled with compacted structural fill and capped with an additional layer of clean fill material and compacted gravel.

The Property was acquired by the City of Port Calloway Redevelopment Authority through eminent domain proceedings concluded in 2012, pursuant to the Authority\'s waterfront revitalization initiative under Connecticut General Statutes § 8-125 *et seq.* Following acquisition, the Authority conducted limited environmental investigation and remedial activities, culminating in the recording of an Environmental Land Use Restriction on the Property in 2018, as described below.

**2.3 Existing Environmental Land Use Restriction (ELUR)**

An Environmental Land Use Restriction (\"ELUR\") was recorded on the Subject Property on March 22, 2018, at Volume 412, Page 88 of the Port Calloway Land Records, pursuant to the Connecticut Remediation Standard Regulations (\"RSRs\"), Conn. Agencies Regs. § 22a-133k-1 *et seq.* The ELUR was approved by CT DEEP following a voluntary remediation action conducted by the Authority in 2016--2017, during which a partial removal of contaminated soils was undertaken and an engineered barrier was installed over portions of the Property where residual contamination remained in near-surface soils above unrestricted-use standards. The ELUR permits industrial and commercial use of the Property and restricts certain other uses, as described below.

The ELUR imposes the following restrictions and obligations on the Subject Property:

> **(a) Prohibition on Ground-Floor Residential Use.** The ELUR prohibits residential use on the ground floor of any structure constructed on the Property. The term \"residential use\" is defined in the ELUR as habitable space at or below finished grade elevation intended for residential dwelling, sleeping, cooking, or eating purposes. This restriction arises from the presence of residual petroleum hydrocarbon contamination in near-surface soils at concentrations exceeding the RSR Residential Direct Exposure Criteria (\"RDECs\"). The ELUR does not define or specifically address non-habitable spaces such as building lobbies, mail rooms, fitness centers, package rooms, leasing offices, or common amenity areas that may serve a residential building but are not themselves dwelling units or habitable residential spaces. This ambiguity is noted for the Client\'s attention, as discussed further below.
>
> **(b) Engineered Barrier Requirement.** Any ground disturbance below a depth of 2 feet below existing grade must be conducted in accordance with a CT DEEP-approved Soil Management Plan. An engineered barrier (cap) consisting of a minimum 24-inch layer of documented clean fill or a geomembrane/concrete barrier system must be maintained over contaminated areas at all times. The ELUR requires that any engineered barrier installed or maintained on the Property be inspected annually and that any breach or compromise of the barrier be reported to CT DEEP within 30 days and repaired within 90 days of discovery.
>
> **(c) Groundwater Use Prohibition.** No installation of potable water supply wells is permitted on the Property. All water supply for any future development must be obtained from municipal water systems.
>
> **(d) Annual Compliance Certification.** The property owner, operator, or designee must submit an annual ELUR compliance certification to CT DEEP, documenting compliance with all ELUR restrictions and confirming the integrity of the engineered barrier.

**Important Note for Client and Client\'s Counsel:** The Client has informed Halcyon that the proposed mixed-use development contemplates a 28-story residential tower with ground-floor commercial retail space, a residential lobby, amenity areas (including a fitness center, resident lounge, and package room), and a leasing office. The ELUR\'s prohibition on ground-floor residential use must be carefully considered in the project design and in any lease agreement governing the development. Halcyon notes that the ELUR restriction applies to \"residential use,\" defined as habitable space intended for residential dwelling, sleeping, cooking, or eating. The ELUR does not, however, expressly define whether ancillary residential spaces --- such as building lobbies, resident amenity rooms, fitness centers, package rooms, and leasing offices that serve a residential tower but do not themselves contain dwelling units --- constitute \"residential use\" within the meaning of the ELUR. This creates a significant interpretive ambiguity that could expose the Client to potential enforcement action by CT DEEP if ground-floor spaces are later determined to fall within the scope of the prohibition.

Halcyon recommends that the Client obtain a formal interpretation or variance from CT DEEP clarifying the permissibility of residential lobby and amenity spaces on the ground floor before finalizing the project design and the ground lease. In the absence of such clarification, the ground lease and project plans should clearly limit ground-floor uses to commercial and retail tenancies and non-habitable ancillary building functions (e.g., mechanical rooms, parking structures, and utility spaces) to avoid potential enforcement action under the ELUR. The Client\'s legal counsel should review the ELUR language in detail and evaluate whether a modification of the ELUR may be required to accommodate the proposed development program.

Additionally, Halcyon understands that the proposed development may include an affordable housing component. Any affordable housing covenant or regulatory agreement applicable to the Property should ensure that affordable dwelling units are located exclusively on upper floors of the residential tower to maintain compliance with the ELUR\'s ground-floor residential use prohibition. Ground-floor placement of any affordable or market-rate dwelling units would be inconsistent with the ELUR and could result in enforcement proceedings by CT DEEP.

**[3. Phase II Investigation Scope and Methodology]{.underline}**

The Phase II ESA field investigation was conducted over a five-day period from April 7 through April 11, 2025. All fieldwork was performed under the direction of Dr. Lena Okafor, Principal Environmental Scientist and Connecticut Licensed Environmental Professional (LEP No. 2241), with the assistance of Halcyon field staff. The investigation scope was designed to evaluate the two areas of concern identified in the Phase I ESA: (1) the northwest corner of the Property in the vicinity of the former UST locations, and (2) the southeastern portion of the Property corresponding to the filled former dry dock basin.

The investigation included the following activities:

> • **Soil Borings:** A total of 22 soil borings (designated SB-1 through SB-22) were advanced to depths ranging from 6 to 20 feet below ground surface (\"bgs\") using a track-mounted Geoprobe 7822DT direct-push drill rig. Borings were positioned to delineate the lateral and vertical extent of potential contamination in the two areas of concern, with additional borings located across the remainder of the Property to confirm background conditions. Boring locations were surveyed using a sub-meter accuracy GPS unit and are depicted on the Boring Location Plan included as Appendix B of the full report.
>
> • **Soil Sampling:** A total of 66 soil samples were collected from selected depth intervals within the borings. Sampling intervals typically included 0--2 feet bgs, 4--6 feet bgs, 8--10 feet bgs, and 15--20 feet bgs, depending on the total depth of each boring and field observations during drilling. Samples were collected in laboratory-supplied containers using dedicated sampling equipment to prevent cross-contamination. All samples were placed on ice immediately after collection and transported to the laboratory under chain-of-custody protocols.
>
> • **Groundwater Monitoring Points:** Six temporary groundwater monitoring points (designated MW-1T through MW-6T) were installed at selected boring locations. Each monitoring point was constructed with a 10-foot length of 1-inch-diameter PVC slotted screen set at approximately 10--20 feet bgs, with a sand pack surrounding the screen interval and a bentonite seal above. The monitoring points were developed by surging and purging prior to sample collection. Groundwater samples were collected approximately 48 hours after development using low-flow sampling techniques in accordance with CT DEEP guidance.
>
> • **Field Screening:** All soil samples were field-screened using a photoionization detector (\"PID\") equipped with a 10.6 eV lamp to provide real-time volatile organic compound concentration data. PID readings were recorded in the field boring logs and used to guide the selection of samples submitted for laboratory analysis.
>
> • **Laboratory Analysis:** All soil and groundwater samples were submitted to Northshore Analytical Laboratories, Inc. (\"Northshore\"), a Connecticut-certified analytical laboratory holding CT DEEP Laboratory Certification No. PH-0287. Laboratory analyses included the following:
>
> • Total Petroleum Hydrocarbons (\"TPH\") by EPA Method 8015 (gasoline-range and diesel-range organics)
>
> • Volatile Organic Compounds (\"VOCs\") by EPA Method 8260
>
> • Semi-Volatile Organic Compounds (\"SVOCs\") by EPA Method 8270
>
> • RCRA 8 Metals by EPA Methods 6010 (ICP) and 7471 (mercury)
>
> • Polychlorinated Biphenyls (\"PCBs\") by EPA Method 8082

All laboratory analyses were performed in accordance with applicable EPA SW-846 methodologies and CT DEEP analytical requirements. Full laboratory analytical reports, including quality assurance/quality control summaries, are provided in Appendix D of the full report.

The investigation focused on the two primary areas of concern, with supplemental sampling across the remainder of the Property to establish baseline conditions and confirm the absence of contamination outside the known impact areas. Borings SB-1 through SB-9 were located in and around the northwest corner former UST area, borings SB-14 through SB-19 were located in and around the southeastern former dry dock area, and borings SB-10 through SB-13 and SB-20 through SB-22 were located across the remainder of the Property, including the waterfront bulkhead area and the central portion of the site.

**[4. Investigation Findings]{.underline}**

**4.1 Contaminated Area 1 --- Northwest Corner (Former UST Area)**

Soil borings advanced in the northwest corner of the Property (SB-1 through SB-9) confirmed the presence of petroleum hydrocarbon contamination in the vicinity of the former underground storage tank locations. The area of soil impact encompasses approximately **4,200 square feet** in the northwest corner of the Property, bounded by borings SB-6 through SB-9 on the perimeter, which served as delineation points.

The primary contaminant of concern identified in this area is Total Petroleum Hydrocarbons (\"TPH\"), consisting predominantly of diesel-range organics (\"DRO\"), consistent with the historical use of this area for diesel fuel and waste oil storage. The maximum TPH concentration detected was **3,800 mg/kg** in soil sample SB-3 at the 4--6 foot bgs interval. Additional elevated TPH results within this area included SB-2 at 2,100 mg/kg (4--6 ft bgs), SB-4 at 1,450 mg/kg (4--6 ft bgs), and SB-5 at 890 mg/kg (8--10 ft bgs). The **applicable Connecticut RSR Residential Direct Exposure Criteria (\"RDEC\") threshold for TPH is 500 mg/kg.** All four borings within the interior of this area exceeded the RDEC threshold at one or more depth intervals.

Notably, TPH concentrations in the 0--2 foot bgs interval were below the 500 mg/kg RDEC in all borings within this area, which is consistent with the historical placement of surface fill and cap material during prior remedial activities. The contamination is concentrated below the existing engineered barrier in the 2-foot to 10-foot bgs depth range. Soil samples collected at 15--20 feet bgs in borings SB-1, SB-3, and SB-5 were below the RDEC threshold, indicating that the vertical extent of contamination does not extend to depth.

Volatile organic compounds were detected at low concentrations in SB-3, specifically benzene at 0.08 mg/kg, which is well below the applicable RSR criterion of 0.4 mg/kg. No other VOC exceedances were identified. Semi-volatile organic compounds, RCRA 8 metals, and polychlorinated biphenyls were all below applicable RSR criteria in all samples collected from this area.

The groundwater sample collected from monitoring point MW-2T, located within the contaminated area, showed dissolved TPH at a concentration of 1.2 mg/L, which is below the applicable groundwater protection criteria of 5.0 mg/L. This result suggests that while petroleum hydrocarbons are present in the subsurface soils, the contamination has not resulted in a significant groundwater plume at this location.

The lateral extent of contamination in Area 1 has been delineated by perimeter borings SB-6 through SB-9, all of which showed TPH concentrations below the 500 mg/kg RDEC, confirming that the contamination is contained within the approximately 4,200-square-foot footprint described above.

**4.2 Contaminated Area 2 --- Former Dry Dock Area**

Soil borings advanced in the southeastern portion of the Property (SB-14 through SB-19) confirmed petroleum hydrocarbon contamination within the fill material placed in the former dry dock basin. The area of soil impact encompasses approximately **1,600 square feet**, corresponding to the central portion of the filled former dry dock basin.

The primary contaminant of concern is Total Petroleum Hydrocarbons, consisting of a mix of gasoline-range organics (\"GRO\") and diesel-range organics (\"DRO\"), consistent with the historical use of the dry dock for vessel hull maintenance, painting, and fueling operations. The maximum TPH concentration detected was **1,200 mg/kg** in soil sample SB-15 at the 6--8 foot bgs interval. Additional elevated TPH results included SB-14 at 780 mg/kg (4--6 ft bgs) and SB-16 at 620 mg/kg (4--6 ft bgs). The **applicable RSR RDEC threshold for TPH is 500 mg/kg.** Three borings exceeded the RDEC in this area.

Low-level naphthalene was detected in SB-15 at a concentration of 0.6 mg/kg. The applicable RSR RDEC criterion for naphthalene is 12 mg/kg; accordingly, this detection is well below the applicable standard and does not represent an exceedance. RCRA 8 metals concentrations were within background ranges in all samples from this area. No PCBs were detected above laboratory reporting limits.

The groundwater sample collected from monitoring point MW-5T showed dissolved TPH at a concentration of 0.4 mg/L, which is well below the applicable groundwater protection criteria of 5.0 mg/L, indicating no significant groundwater impact in this area.

The vertical extent of contamination is concentrated between 4 feet and 10 feet bgs, within the fill material placed in the former dry dock basin. Samples collected at shallower and deeper intervals were below RDEC thresholds. The lateral extent of contamination has been delineated by surrounding borings SB-17 through SB-19, all of which showed TPH concentrations below 500 mg/kg, confirming that the contamination is contained within the approximately 1,600-square-foot footprint.

**4.3 Remainder of Property**

Soil samples collected from the ten borings located outside the two identified contamination areas --- specifically SB-10 through SB-13, SB-20 through SB-22, and selected perimeter delineation borings --- showed all analytes below applicable Connecticut RSR criteria. No exceedances of RDEC or industrial/commercial direct exposure criteria were identified in any sample from these locations.

Groundwater samples collected from monitoring points MW-1T, MW-3T, MW-4T, and MW-6T showed no exceedances of applicable groundwater quality criteria for any analyzed parameter. Dissolved TPH concentrations in these samples ranged from non-detect to 0.2 mg/L, well below the 5.0 mg/L criterion.

No evidence of contamination was identified in the bulkhead area along the eastern boundary of the Property. Petroleum-stained fill was noted visually in boring SB-20 at the 2--4 foot bgs interval, and the PID reading at this location was 15 ppm. However, laboratory analysis of this sample confirmed TPH at a concentration of 180 mg/kg, which is well below the 500 mg/kg RDEC and does not constitute an exceedance. No polychlorinated biphenyls were detected above laboratory reporting limits in any soil or groundwater sample collected during the investigation.

**[5. Flood Zone and Coastal Considerations]{.underline}**

The Subject Property is located within **FEMA Flood Zone AE** as identified on the Federal Emergency Management Agency (\"FEMA\") Flood Insurance Rate Map (\"FIRM\") Panel No. 09009C0301G, with an effective date of January 15, 2020. Flood Zone AE is defined as an area subject to inundation by the 1-percent-annual-chance flood event (the 100-year flood), for which base flood elevations have been determined. The **Base Flood Elevation (\"BFE\") applicable to the Subject Property is 12 feet NAVD88.**

Existing site grade elevations across the Subject Property range from approximately 9 feet NAVD88 at the waterfront bulkhead line along the eastern boundary to approximately 14 feet NAVD88 at the Pier Street/Harbor Avenue intersection in the northwest corner. A significant portion of the Property, particularly the eastern half fronting the waterfront, lies below the BFE of 12 feet NAVD88, and is therefore within the regulatory floodplain.

The Client\'s proposed development plans, as shared with Halcyon for purposes of this Assessment, indicate a proposed **finished floor elevation (\"FFE\") of 15 feet NAVD88** for the ground-floor level of the proposed mixed-use structure. This would provide **3 feet of freeboard** above the established BFE of 12 feet NAVD88, which satisfies the minimum requirements of the current Connecticut Building Code and the National Flood Insurance Program (\"NFIP\") for new construction in Flood Zone AE.

**Observation Regarding Coastal Resilience Standards:** Halcyon notes that recent Connecticut regulatory and legislative developments have increased attention to coastal resilience and sea level rise adaptation in the design and construction of new waterfront development. Specifically, **Connecticut Public Act 23-167 (2023)**, *An Act Concerning Climate Change Adaptation*, requires state-funded projects in coastal areas to incorporate sea level rise projections into project design, planning, and construction decision-making. While it is not certain whether this statute applies directly to a privately developed project on Authority-owned land subject to a long-term ground lease, the legislative trend is clear, and a number of Connecticut municipal authorities --- including those in coastal Fairfield and New Haven counties --- have adopted or are actively considering requirements for **4 to 5 feet of freeboard above BFE for new construction in flood zones**, reflecting updated sea level rise projections published by the National Oceanic and Atmospheric Administration (\"NOAA\") and the Connecticut Institute for Resilience and Climate Adaptation (\"CIRCA\"). CIRCA\'s 2019 sea level rise projections for Connecticut indicate a potential rise of 20 inches by 2050 and up to 80 inches by 2100 under high-emission scenarios.

**Halcyon recommends that the Client carefully evaluate whether the proposed 3-foot freeboard (FFE of 15 feet NAVD88) is sufficient under current and reasonably anticipated future regulatory requirements, particularly given the 99-year intended lease term** of the proposed ground lease and the potential for BFE revisions as FEMA updates its flood mapping in response to changing coastal conditions. A higher FFE --- in the range of 16 to 17 feet NAVD88, providing 4 to 5 feet of freeboard above the current BFE --- may be advisable as a long-term risk mitigation measure and to ensure continued compliance with evolving coastal resilience standards over the life of the development.

**Construction Considerations:** The waterfront location of the Subject Property and its designation within FEMA Flood Zone AE present a tangible risk of construction delays due to coastal storm events, storm surge, and tidal flooding. Halcyon notes that the Property experienced tidal flooding during a significant nor\'easter event in November 2024, during which water levels reached approximately 10.5 feet NAVD88 at the bulkhead along the eastern boundary. During the April 2025 field investigation, Halcyon observed evidence of recent high-water marks on the bulkhead structure and adjacent grade areas consistent with this reported flooding event. Halcyon recommends that any development agreement --- including the proposed ground lease and any construction contracts --- account for the potential for weather-related construction delays, particularly during the Atlantic hurricane season (June through November). Given the Property\'s direct coastal exposure and the well-documented increasing frequency and intensity of significant storm events affecting Long Island Sound and the southern Connecticut coastline, construction scheduling and contractual force majeure provisions should be carefully calibrated to reflect the realistic probability of storm-related interruptions over the multi-year construction period.

The approximately 480 linear feet of timber and reinforced concrete bulkhead along the eastern boundary of the Property appeared to be in fair to poor condition during Halcyon\'s site inspection. Several bulkhead sections exhibited lateral displacement, longitudinal and transverse cracking, deteriorated and missing timber lagging, and evidence of erosion of backfill material behind the bulkhead wall. The structural integrity of the bulkhead is a material concern for any waterfront development on this Property. Halcyon recommends that bulkhead rehabilitation or replacement be incorporated into the development plan and that an independent structural engineering assessment of the bulkhead be commissioned to determine the scope and cost of necessary repairs. Bulkhead repair or replacement costs are not included in the environmental remediation cost estimates presented in Section 6 below.

**[6. Remediation Cost Estimates]{.underline}**

Based on the investigation findings described in Section 4, Halcyon has prepared preliminary remediation cost estimates for addressing the two identified contamination areas at the Subject Property. These estimates assume that remediation will be performed in conjunction with site development earthwork and grading activities, which is anticipated to result in cost efficiencies relative to a standalone remediation project. The estimates are intended to support the Client\'s due diligence evaluation and the negotiation of remediation cost allocation within the proposed ground lease.

**Contaminated Area 1 --- Northwest Corner (Former UST Area)**

The recommended remediation approach for Area 1 is excavation and off-site disposal of contaminated soil within the approximately 4,200-square-foot impacted area. Based on the vertical extent of contamination documented in the investigation (concentrated between 2 and 10 feet bgs), the estimated volume of impacted soil requiring excavation is approximately 933 cubic yards (4,200 SF × average 6 ft depth ÷ 27 CF/CY). Including additional volume for necessary over-excavation beyond the delineated impact boundaries, temporary shoring and excavation support, and clean backfill handling, the total estimated material handling volume is approximately 3,100 cubic yards.

An alternative remediation approach --- in-situ chemical treatment with maintenance of an engineered barrier --- was evaluated but is not recommended as the primary approach because it would impose limitations on future subsurface construction, including foundation work, utility installation, and subgrade parking structures, within the impacted area. Excavation and removal provides a more definitive and permanent remedy that is compatible with the Client\'s proposed development program.

**Estimated Cost for Area 1 Remediation (Excavation and Disposal): \$1,850,000**

  -----------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------
  **Cost Component**                                          **Estimated Cost**
  ----------------------------------------------------------- -----------------------------------
  Excavation and soil management                              \$680,000

  Off-site transportation and disposal at licensed facility   \$520,000

  Confirmation sampling and laboratory analysis               \$85,000

  Clean backfill procurement, placement, and compaction       \$290,000

  Contingency (10%)                                           \$100,000

  **Total --- Area 1**                                        **\$1,850,000**
  -----------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------

**Contaminated Area 2 --- Former Dry Dock Area**

The recommended remediation approach for Area 2 is excavation and off-site disposal of approximately 600 cubic yards of contaminated fill material within the approximately 1,600-square-foot former dry dock footprint. The fill material in the dry dock basin is anticipated to be relatively accessible for excavation given the open site conditions and the shallow depth of the impacted zone (4--10 feet bgs within the fill).

**Estimated Cost for Area 2 Remediation (Excavation and Disposal): \$550,000**

  -----------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------
  **Cost Component**                                          **Estimated Cost**
  ----------------------------------------------------------- -----------------------------------
  Excavation and soil management                              \$210,000

  Off-site transportation and disposal at licensed facility   \$145,000

  Confirmation sampling and laboratory analysis               \$40,000

  Clean backfill procurement, placement, and compaction       \$85,000

  Environmental oversight, field management, and reporting    \$45,000

  Contingency (10%)                                           \$25,000

  **Total --- Area 2**                                        **\$550,000**
  -----------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------

**Total Estimated Remediation Cost**

**Total Estimated Remediation Cost: \$2,400,000** (\$1,850,000 for Area 1 + \$550,000 for Area 2).

These estimates are based on the following key assumptions: (i) remediation is performed in conjunction with site development earthwork, allowing shared mobilization and equipment costs; (ii) a CT DEEP-approved Remedial Action Plan (\"RAP\") is in place prior to commencement of remediation activities; (iii) contaminated soil is transported to and disposed of at a licensed solid waste disposal or treatment facility in Connecticut or a neighboring state; and (iv) groundwater dewatering and treatment are not required during excavation. Costs could increase materially if contamination is found to extend beyond the delineated areas during excavation, if unanticipated contaminants are encountered, or if groundwater dewatering and on-site treatment are required to maintain dry working conditions during excavation.

These cost estimates do not include the cost of maintaining or modifying the existing ELUR, obtaining any necessary CT DEEP approvals or permits, preparing the required Remedial Action Plan and post-remediation Verification Report, or any legal or consulting fees associated with ELUR compliance. These cost estimates also do not include the cost of bulkhead repair or replacement, which should be estimated separately based on the recommended structural engineering assessment.

**Allocation Note:** Halcyon understands from the Client that the parties to the proposed ground lease transaction are negotiating the allocation of environmental remediation costs between the Authority (as Landlord) and the Client (as Tenant). The Client has indicated that the Authority has agreed to provide a **\$1,800,000 credit** against lease rent payments to offset remediation costs, which would leave approximately **\$600,000** (\$2,400,000 − \$1,800,000 = \$600,000) as the Tenant\'s financial responsibility for environmental remediation. Halcyon takes no position on the appropriateness of this allocation but notes the figures here for the completeness of this executive summary and to facilitate the Client\'s financial due diligence.

**[7. Conclusions and Recommendations]{.underline}**

**Conclusions.** The Phase II Environmental Site Assessment confirmed the presence of petroleum hydrocarbon contamination in two discrete areas of the Subject Property, both attributable to the Property\'s historical use as a ship repair and dry dock facility from approximately 1942 through 1987. Both contamination areas exceed Connecticut RSR Residential Direct Exposure Criteria for Total Petroleum Hydrocarbons, with maximum concentrations of 3,800 mg/kg in Area 1 (Northwest Corner / Former UST Area) and 1,200 mg/kg in Area 2 (Former Dry Dock Area), compared to the applicable RDEC threshold of 500 mg/kg.

The contamination in both areas is laterally and vertically delineated based on the sampling program. Perimeter borings in both areas showed TPH concentrations below the 500 mg/kg RDEC, and samples at deeper intervals (15--20 feet bgs) were below applicable thresholds. Groundwater sampling results indicate that the petroleum hydrocarbon contamination has not resulted in significant groundwater impact, and the contamination does not appear to have migrated off-site based on the available data.

The existing ELUR recorded at Volume 412, Page 88 of the Port Calloway Land Records imposes land use restrictions that are consistent with the investigation findings. The ELUR must be maintained unless the Property is fully remediated to unrestricted-use standards under the Connecticut RSRs, which would require significantly greater remediation expenditures than the estimates presented in this report and is not currently contemplated by the Client.

**Recommendations.** Based on the findings of this Phase II ESA, Halcyon provides the following recommendations for the Client\'s consideration:

> **1. Remediation.** Proceed with excavation and off-site disposal of contaminated soils in both Area 1 (approximately 3,100 cubic yards) and Area 2 (approximately 600 cubic yards) in conjunction with site development earthwork. All remediation activities should be conducted under a CT DEEP-approved Remedial Action Plan, with confirmation sampling to verify that post-excavation conditions meet applicable RSR criteria. The estimated total remediation cost is \$2,400,000, subject to the assumptions and qualifications stated in Section 6 above.
>
> **2. ELUR Compliance --- Ground-Floor Residential Use Restriction.** Ensure that the proposed development design and any ground lease agreement are fully consistent with the ELUR\'s restrictions, particularly the prohibition on ground-floor residential use. As discussed in Section 2.3 of this report, the ELUR prohibits residential use on the ground floor but does not expressly address non-habitable ancillary spaces such as residential lobbies, fitness centers, amenity rooms, and leasing offices. The Client should seek formal clarification from CT DEEP regarding the permissibility of residential lobby and amenity spaces on the ground floor before finalizing the project design and lease terms. In the absence of such clarification, ground-floor uses should be limited to commercial, retail, and clearly non-habitable ancillary building functions. Additionally, any affordable housing units included in the development should be located exclusively on upper floors of the residential tower to ensure compliance with the ELUR prohibition.
>
> **3. Engineered Barrier.** Maintain or reconstruct an engineered barrier (cap) over contaminated areas in accordance with the ELUR requirements. Construction plans should incorporate the ELUR-required 24-inch layer of documented clean fill or an equivalent geomembrane/concrete barrier system, with provisions for inspection, maintenance, and repair. The development\'s site grading and foundation design should be coordinated with the engineered barrier requirements to ensure that the barrier is not compromised during or after construction.
>
> **4. Soil Management Plan.** Develop and obtain CT DEEP approval of a Soil Management Plan (\"SMP\") prior to any ground disturbance on the Subject Property. The SMP should address procedures for handling, characterizing, stockpiling, and disposing of soil encountered during construction, including protocols for unexpected contamination discovery, worker health and safety, dust control, and stormwater management during excavation activities.
>
> **5. Flood Resilience and Freeboard.** Evaluate whether the proposed 3-foot freeboard (FFE of 15 feet NAVD88 above BFE of 12 feet NAVD88) is adequate for the 99-year anticipated lease term, given evolving Connecticut coastal resilience standards and sea level rise projections. As discussed in Section 5, recent legislative developments (including Connecticut Public Act 23-167) and emerging municipal standards in coastal Connecticut communities suggest that 4 to 5 feet of freeboard may become the standard for new waterfront construction. Consider increasing the FFE to 16--17 feet NAVD88 (providing 4--5 feet of freeboard) as a long-term risk mitigation measure. Additionally, the proposed ground lease and construction agreements should include force majeure provisions that are specifically calibrated for the risk of weather-related construction delays at this coastal site, including tidal flooding, storm surge, and hurricane events.
>
> **6. Environmental Insurance.** Obtain environmental liability insurance, specifically a pollution legal liability (\"PLL\") policy, to cover potential unknown contamination conditions, cost overruns related to remediation, and third-party claims arising from the historical contamination at the Property. Coverage should be tailored to the specific risks identified in this Assessment and should extend for the duration of the remediation and construction period, with consideration of a longer policy term given the long-term nature of the proposed ground lease.
>
> **7. Ongoing Monitoring.** Following completion of remediation activities, implement a post-remediation groundwater monitoring program as may be required by CT DEEP as a condition of the Remedial Action Plan or ELUR compliance. The monitoring program should include periodic sampling of groundwater quality at established monitoring points to confirm that residual contamination is stable and is not migrating toward the Long Island Sound waterfront or adjacent properties.
>
> **8. Bulkhead Assessment.** Commission an independent structural engineering assessment of the existing approximately 480-linear-foot bulkhead along the eastern boundary of the Property to determine the scope and cost of rehabilitation or replacement. The bulkhead is in fair to poor condition based on Halcyon\'s visual observations and represents a material structural and financial consideration for the proposed waterfront development. Bulkhead repair or replacement costs are not included in the environmental remediation cost estimates presented in this report.

**[8. Limitations and Qualifications]{.underline}**

This executive summary is subject to the limitations, qualifications, and assumptions set forth in the full Phase II Environmental Site Assessment report (Halcyon Project No. HEC-2025-0412), which should be reviewed in its entirety for a complete understanding of the investigation methodology, data, findings, and professional opinions presented herein.

The findings and conclusions presented in this report are based on conditions observed and samples collected during the field investigation conducted on April 7--11, 2025. Subsurface conditions are inherently variable and may differ between sampling points and across the Property. The sampling program was designed to provide a reasonable level of characterization of the identified areas of concern, but cannot guarantee that all contamination has been identified or that conditions between borings are identical to those at the sampled locations.

Remediation cost estimates presented in Section 6 are preliminary, opinion-level estimates prepared by Halcyon based on the data available as of the report date. These estimates are intended for planning and due diligence purposes and are subject to change based on actual field conditions encountered during remediation, evolving regulatory requirements, contractor availability and pricing, disposal facility costs, and other market conditions at the time remediation is performed. Halcyon makes no warranty or guarantee that actual remediation costs will not exceed the estimates provided.

This report was prepared for the exclusive use of Meridian Gateway Holdings LLC and its authorized agents, legal counsel, and lenders as specifically identified in Section 1. No other party is authorized to rely on this report or its findings without Halcyon\'s prior written consent, executed by a duly authorized officer of the firm. Any reliance by unauthorized third parties is at their own risk.

This Assessment does not constitute a legal opinion regarding compliance with any federal, state, or local environmental law, regulation, or ordinance. The Client is advised to consult with qualified legal counsel regarding ELUR compliance, regulatory obligations, and the legal implications of the environmental conditions documented in this report for the proposed ground lease transaction and development.

**RESOLUTION NO. 2025-047**

**OF THE BOARD OF COMMISSIONERS** **OF THE CITY OF PORT CALLOWAY REDEVELOPMENT AUTHORITY**

Adopted at a Duly Noticed Special Meeting Held on June 5, 2025

75 Municipal Plaza, Port Calloway, CT 06801

**[PREAMBLE AND ROLL CALL]{.underline}**

A quorum of the Board of Commissioners of the City of Port Calloway Redevelopment Authority (the \"Authority\"), a public body corporate and politic created and existing under Connecticut General Statutes § 8-125, being duly present, the special meeting was called to order by Commissioner Diana Forsythe, Chair. The Chair confirmed that proper notice of the special meeting had been given in accordance with the Connecticut Freedom of Information Act and the Authority\'s bylaws. Howard Koss of Pryor Whitfield & Koss LLP, 55 Courthouse Square, Port Calloway, CT 06801, legal counsel to the Authority, was present and advised the Board throughout the proceedings.

**[RECITALS]{.underline}**

**WHEREAS**, the Authority was established in 2008 under Connecticut General Statutes § 8-125 for the purpose of overseeing the revitalization of Port Calloway\'s 47-acre waterfront district, and the Authority has since that time been engaged in planning, land acquisition, environmental remediation, and developer solicitation activities in furtherance of that mission; and

**WHEREAS**, the Authority holds fee simple title to a 3.2-acre (139,392 square foot) waterfront parcel located at 10-30 Pier Street, Port Calloway, CT 06801, identified as Assessor\'s Parcel No. 127-003-0045 (the \"Parcel\"), situated within the Port Calloway Waterfront Revitalization District, zoned WRD-3 (Mixed-Use High Density), which Parcel was acquired by the Authority through eminent domain proceedings concluded in 2012 and is currently unimproved; and

**WHEREAS**, Meridian Gateway Holdings LLC, a Delaware limited liability company with its principal place of business at 400 Harborview Drive, Suite 1200, Port Calloway, CT 06801 (\"Meridian\" or \"Tenant\"), has proposed to develop a mixed-use project on the Parcel comprising a 28-story residential tower, a 6-story Class A office building, and ground-floor retail space (collectively, the \"Project\"), representing a total project cost of approximately Four Hundred Twenty-Five Million Dollars (\$425,000,000); and

**WHEREAS**, Meridian was formed in 2019 by developer Marcus Ellison, its Managing Member, and institutional partner Coventry Capital Partners LP, a Delaware limited partnership, and Meridian and its principals have developed over \$1.8 billion in mixed-use projects across the Northeast, demonstrating substantial experience and financial capacity relevant to the Project; and

**WHEREAS**, the Authority, through its Executive Director, Paul Castignetti, and with the advice of the Authority\'s legal counsel, Pryor Whitfield & Koss LLP, has negotiated a term sheet dated June 10, 2025 (the \"Term Sheet\") with Meridian setting forth the principal terms and conditions for a long-term ground lease of the Parcel for a term of ninety-nine (99) years, commencing on or about October 1, 2025 (the \"Ground Lease\"), which Term Sheet has been provided to the Board for its review in advance of this meeting; and

**WHEREAS**, the Term Sheet provides for, among other things: (a) an initial annual base rent of Two Million Eight Hundred Fifty Thousand Dollars (\$2,850,000) per year, with periodic escalations as set forth therein; (b) percentage rent equal to 2.0% of gross revenues above a Twenty-Eight Million Five Hundred Thousand Dollar (\$28,500,000) annual breakpoint commencing in Year 6 of the Ground Lease term; (c) a security deposit in the form of a Five Million Seven Hundred Thousand Dollar (\$5,700,000) irrevocable standby letter of credit issued by a federally chartered banking institution; (d) a remediation credit of One Million Eight Hundred Thousand Dollars (\$1,800,000) to be applied against initial rent payments in recognition of Tenant\'s assumption of certain environmental remediation responsibilities; and (e) development milestones with reverter rights in favor of the Authority in the event of Tenant\'s failure to achieve such milestones within the prescribed time periods; and

**WHEREAS**, the Authority is aware that the Parcel has recognized environmental conditions resulting from its former use as a ship repair facility (1942--1987), as documented in the Phase I Environmental Site Assessment dated March 15, 2025, and the Phase II Environmental Site Assessment dated May 2, 2025, both prepared by Halcyon Environmental Consultants Inc., and that an Environmental Land Use Restriction (\"ELUR\") was recorded on March 22, 2018, at Volume 412, Page 88 of the Port Calloway Land Records, which restricts certain uses of the Parcel and imposes obligations with respect to the management of residual contamination; and

**WHEREAS**, Meridian has secured a construction loan commitment in the amount of Two Hundred Eighty-Five Million Dollars (\$285,000,000) from Bayside Federal Lending Corp. and equity commitments of Ninety-Five Million Dollars (\$95,000,000) from Coventry Capital Partners LP, and the Ground Lease must contain provisions satisfactory to the construction lender to enable financing of the Project, including customary leasehold mortgage protections and subordination, non-disturbance, and attornment provisions; and

**WHEREAS**, the development of the Parcel is a critical component of the Authority\'s waterfront revitalization initiative and will generate substantial economic benefits to the City of Port Calloway, including the creation of significant construction and permanent employment opportunities, increased tax revenue based on a projected post-development assessed value of One Hundred Seventy-Eight Million Dollars (\$178,000,000), activation of the waterfront promenade and pedestrian access corridors, and the provision of new housing, office, and retail space within the waterfront district; and

**WHEREAS**, consistent with the Authority\'s mission and the restrictive covenant recorded against the Parcel, the Project must include not fewer than fifteen percent (15%) of the residential units as affordable housing units, affordable to households earning at or below eighty percent (80%) of Area Median Income (\"AMI\"), for the duration of the Ground Lease; and

**WHEREAS**, the Project must include a minimum of 8,000 square feet of publicly accessible open space on the waterfront side of the Parcel, connected to the existing public pedestrian promenade, to ensure continued public access to and enjoyment of the waterfront; and

**WHEREAS**, the Authority supports a 15-year tax abatement for the Project, phasing in assessments at 25% of full assessment for Years 1 through 5, 50% of full assessment for Years 6 through 10, and 75% of full assessment for Years 11 through 15, with full assessment thereafter, to be implemented through a separate tax abatement agreement between Meridian and the City of Port Calloway; and

**WHEREAS**, the Authority\'s legal counsel, Pryor Whitfield & Koss LLP, has reviewed the Term Sheet and has advised the Board that the proposed transaction is within the Authority\'s statutory powers under Connecticut General Statutes § 8-125 *et seq.* and is consistent with the Authority\'s adopted waterfront revitalization plan, as most recently amended and readopted in 2022; and

**WHEREAS**, the Board has determined that the Ground Lease serves a valid public purpose by facilitating the redevelopment of a contaminated, underutilized waterfront parcel into a vibrant mixed-use community consistent with the public interest, and that the economic terms of the Ground Lease are fair and reasonable to the Authority and the residents of Port Calloway;

**[OPERATIVE PROVISIONS]{.underline}**

**NOW, THEREFORE, BE IT RESOLVED** by the Board of Commissioners of the City of Port Calloway Redevelopment Authority as follows:

**Section 1. Authorization to Execute Ground Lease.** The Executive Director, Paul Castignetti, is hereby authorized and directed, on behalf of the Authority, to negotiate, execute, and deliver a Ground Lease Agreement with Meridian Gateway Holdings LLC for the Parcel, on terms and conditions substantially consistent with the Term Sheet dated June 10, 2025, for a term of ninety-nine (99) years commencing on or about October 1, 2025, and expiring September 30, 2124, at an initial annual base rent of Two Million Eight Hundred Fifty Thousand Dollars (\$2,850,000) per annum, subject to escalation and adjustment as set forth in the Term Sheet, including the percentage rent, remediation credit, and security deposit provisions described therein.

**Section 2. Required Lease Provisions.** The Ground Lease shall include, without limitation, the following provisions:

> \(a\) development milestones, including commencement and completion deadlines for each phase of the Project, with reverter rights in favor of the Authority in the event of Tenant\'s failure to achieve such milestones within the prescribed time periods;
>
> \(b\) a requirement that not fewer than fifteen percent (15%) of the residential units in the Project be designated as affordable housing units for households earning at or below eighty percent (80%) of Area Median Income for the duration of the Ground Lease;
>
> \(c\) insurance requirements satisfactory to the Authority, including commercial general liability, property, builder\'s risk, and such other coverages as the Authority may reasonably require;
>
> \(d\) compliance with the Environmental Land Use Restriction recorded at Volume 412, Page 88 of the Port Calloway Land Records, including any obligations relating to the management, monitoring, and reporting of residual environmental contamination on the Parcel;
>
> \(e\) a minimum of 8,000 square feet of publicly accessible open space on the waterfront side of the Parcel, connected to the existing public pedestrian promenade, with maintenance obligations to be borne by Tenant;
>
> \(f\) provisions requiring the Project to comply with all applicable zoning, building, environmental, and other governmental requirements; and
>
> \(g\) such other terms, conditions, and provisions as the Executive Director, in consultation with the Authority\'s legal counsel, deems necessary or appropriate to protect the interests of the Authority and to effectuate the purposes of this Resolution.

**Section 3. Authorization of Related Documents.** The Executive Director is further authorized and directed to execute and deliver, on behalf of the Authority, such other documents and instruments as may be necessary or appropriate to consummate the transaction contemplated by this Resolution, including, without limitation:

> \(a\) a Subordination, Non-Disturbance, and Attornment Agreement with Bayside Federal Lending Corp. or any other leasehold mortgagee approved by the Authority in accordance with the terms of the Ground Lease;
>
> \(b\) a memorandum of lease in recordable form for filing in the Port Calloway Land Records;
>
> \(c\) estoppel certificates as may be reasonably requested by Meridian or its lenders from time to time during the term of the Ground Lease; and
>
> \(d\) any tax abatement agreement with the City of Port Calloway on terms consistent with the phased assessment structure described in the recitals hereto.

**Section 4. Delegation of Authority.** The Executive Director is authorized to approve such changes, modifications, and amendments to the terms and conditions of the Ground Lease and the related documents as the Executive Director, in consultation with the Authority\'s legal counsel, determines to be immaterial or otherwise in the best interest of the Authority; *provided, however*, that:

> \(a\) the initial annual base rent shall not be reduced below Two Million Eight Hundred Fifty Thousand Dollars (\$2,850,000);
>
> \(b\) the lease term shall not exceed ninety-nine (99) years;
>
> \(c\) the affordable housing requirement of not fewer than fifteen percent (15%) of the residential units at or below eighty percent (80%) of Area Median Income shall not be reduced or eliminated; and
>
> \(d\) any deviation from the Term Sheet that the Executive Director or the Authority\'s legal counsel determines to be material shall be brought before the Board for further review and approval prior to execution.

**Section 5. Effective Date.** This Resolution shall take effect immediately upon its adoption.

**[CERTIFICATION]{.underline}**

I hereby certify that the foregoing Resolution No. 2025-047 was duly adopted by the Board of Commissioners of the City of Port Calloway Redevelopment Authority at a special meeting duly noticed and held on June 5, 2025, at which a quorum was present and acting throughout, by a vote of **\_\_ in favor, \_** *opposed, and* **\_**\_\_ abstaining, and that said Resolution has not been amended, modified, or rescinded since its adoption and is in full force and effect as of the date set forth below.

"""Lightweight legal-document builder: marker text -> styled .docx"""
import re, sys
from docx import Document
from docx.shared import Pt, Inches, RGBColor
from docx.enum.text import WD_ALIGN_PARAGRAPH, WD_BREAK
from docx.enum.table import WD_TABLE_ALIGNMENT
from docx.enum.section import WD_SECTION
from docx.oxml.ns import qn
from docx.oxml import OxmlElement

BODY_FONT = "Times New Roman"

def set_cell_border(cell, **kwargs):
    tc = cell._tc
    tcPr = tc.get_or_add_tcPr()
    tcBorders = tcPr.find(qn('w:tcBorders'))
    if tcBorders is None:
        tcBorders = OxmlElement('w:tcBorders')
        tcPr.append(tcBorders)
    for edge in ('top','bottom','left','right'):
        if edge in kwargs:
            ed = kwargs[edge]
            el = tcBorders.find(qn('w:'+edge))
            if el is None:
                el = OxmlElement('w:'+edge)
                tcBorders.append(el)
            for k,v in ed.items():
                el.set(qn('w:'+k), str(v))

def shade(cell, fill):
    tcPr = cell._tc.get_or_add_tcPr()
    shd = OxmlElement('w:shd')
    shd.set(qn('w:val'), 'clear'); shd.set(qn('w:color'), 'auto'); shd.set(qn('w:fill'), fill)
    tcPr.append(shd)

def add_page_number_footer(section, left_text=""):
    footer = section.footer
    p = footer.paragraphs[0]
    p.text = ""
    p.alignment = WD_ALIGN_PARAGRAPH.CENTER
    if left_text:
        r0 = p.add_run(left_text + "\t\t")
        r0.font.size = Pt(8); r0.font.name = BODY_FONT
    r = p.add_run("Page ")
    r.font.size = Pt(8); r.font.name = BODY_FONT
    fld = OxmlElement('w:fldSimple'); fld.set(qn('w:instr'), 'PAGE')
    rr = OxmlElement('w:r'); rpr = OxmlElement('w:rPr')
    sz = OxmlElement('w:sz'); sz.set(qn('w:val'), '16'); rpr.append(sz)
    rf = OxmlElement('w:rFonts'); rf.set(qn('w:ascii'), BODY_FONT); rf.set(qn('w:hAnsi'), BODY_FONT); rpr.append(rf)
    rr.append(rpr); t = OxmlElement('w:t'); t.text = "1"; rr.append(t); fld.append(rr)
    p._p.append(fld)
    r2 = p.add_run(" of ")
    r2.font.size = Pt(8); r2.font.name = BODY_FONT
    fld2 = OxmlElement('w:fldSimple'); fld2.set(qn('w:instr'), 'NUMPAGES')
    rr2 = OxmlElement('w:r'); rpr2 = OxmlElement('w:rPr')
    sz2 = OxmlElement('w:sz'); sz2.set(qn('w:val'), '16'); rpr2.append(sz2)
    rf2 = OxmlElement('w:rFonts'); rf2.set(qn('w:ascii'), BODY_FONT); rf2.set(qn('w:hAnsi'), BODY_FONT); rpr2.append(rf2)
    rr2.append(rpr2); t2 = OxmlElement('w:t'); t2.text = "1"; rr2.append(t2); fld2.append(rr2)
    p._p.append(fld2)

INLINE = re.compile(r'(\*\*.+?\*\*|__.+?__)')
def add_inline(p, text, size=11, bold=False, italic=False, font=BODY_FONT, color=None):
    for part in INLINE.split(text):
        if not part:
            continue
        b, i = bold, italic
        if part.startswith('**') and part.endswith('**') and len(part) > 4:
            part = part[2:-2]; b = True
        elif part.startswith('__') and part.endswith('__') and len(part) > 4:
            part = part[2:-2]; i = True
        r = p.add_run(part)
        r.font.name = font
        r.font.size = Pt(size)
        r.bold = b; r.italic = i
        if color: r.font.color.rgb = color

def build(src, out, footer_left="", title_page_toc=False, base_size=11):
    doc = Document()
    st = doc.styles['Normal']
    st.font.name = BODY_FONT
    st.font.size = Pt(base_size)
    st.element.rPr.rFonts.set(qn('w:eastAsia'), BODY_FONT)
    pf = st.paragraph_format
    pf.space_after = Pt(6); pf.space_before = Pt(0)
    pf.line_spacing = 1.0

    sec = doc.sections[0]
    sec.top_margin = Inches(1.0); sec.bottom_margin = Inches(1.0)
    sec.left_margin = Inches(1.0); sec.right_margin = Inches(1.0)
    add_page_number_footer(sec, footer_left)

    lines = open(src, encoding='utf-8').read().split('\n')
    i = 0
    # optional TOC of H1s
    if title_page_toc:
        h1s = [l[4:].strip() for l in lines if l.startswith('@H1 ')]
    while i < len(lines):
        raw = lines[i]; i += 1
        line = raw.rstrip()
        if not line.strip():
            continue
        if line.startswith('@'):
            tag, _, rest = line.partition(' ')
        else:
            tag, rest = '@P', line
        cmd = tag[1:]
        if cmd == 'TITLE':
            p = doc.add_paragraph(); p.alignment = WD_ALIGN_PARAGRAPH.CENTER
            p.paragraph_format.space_before = Pt(0); p.paragraph_format.space_after = Pt(10)
            add_inline(p, rest, size=16, bold=True)
        elif cmd == 'SUBTITLE':
            p = doc.add_paragraph(); p.alignment = WD_ALIGN_PARAGRAPH.CENTER
            p.paragraph_format.space_after = Pt(8)
            add_inline(p, rest, size=11.5, bold=True)
        elif cmd == 'CENTER':
            p = doc.add_paragraph(); p.alignment = WD_ALIGN_PARAGRAPH.CENTER
            add_inline(p, rest, size=base_size)
        elif cmd == 'CENTERB':
            p = doc.add_paragraph(); p.alignment = WD_ALIGN_PARAGRAPH.CENTER
            add_inline(p, rest, size=base_size, bold=True)
        elif cmd == 'H1':
            p = doc.add_paragraph(); p.alignment = WD_ALIGN_PARAGRAPH.CENTER
            p.paragraph_format.space_before = Pt(16); p.paragraph_format.space_after = Pt(10)
            p.paragraph_format.keep_with_next = True
            add_inline(p, rest, size=base_size, bold=True)
        elif cmd == 'H1L':
            p = doc.add_paragraph(); p.alignment = WD_ALIGN_PARAGRAPH.LEFT
            p.paragraph_format.space_before = Pt(16); p.paragraph_format.space_after = Pt(8)
            p.paragraph_format.keep_with_next = True
            add_inline(p, rest, size=base_size, bold=True)
        elif cmd == 'H2':
            p = doc.add_paragraph(); p.alignment = WD_ALIGN_PARAGRAPH.LEFT
            p.paragraph_format.space_before = Pt(10); p.paragraph_format.space_after = Pt(4)
            p.paragraph_format.keep_with_next = True
            add_inline(p, rest, size=base_size, bold=True)
        elif cmd == 'H3':
            p = doc.add_paragraph(); p.alignment = WD_ALIGN_PARAGRAPH.LEFT
            p.paragraph_format.space_before = Pt(8); p.paragraph_format.space_after = Pt(3)
            p.paragraph_format.keep_with_next = True
            add_inline(p, rest, size=base_size, bold=True, italic=True)
        elif cmd == 'P':
            p = doc.add_paragraph(); p.alignment = WD_ALIGN_PARAGRAPH.JUSTIFY
            add_inline(p, rest, size=base_size)
        elif cmd == 'PL':
            p = doc.add_paragraph(); p.alignment = WD_ALIGN_PARAGRAPH.LEFT
            add_inline(p, rest, size=base_size)
        elif cmd == 'PB':

VI. CONNECTICUT LAW: FORFEITURE, PENALTIES, AND REMEDIES

      The following is a doctrinal summary prepared for negotiation purposes. It is not a
      legal opinion. The specific authorities should be confirmed by citator, and by a
      Connecticut litigation partner, before any of it is used in correspondence, a demand,
      or a brief. See Section 2.3.

6.1 The two doctrines that bear on the reverter
A reverter that transfers $300 million of improvements to the Authority on a missed
date is exposed on two independent lines of attack, and a third that is weaker but
worth preserving.
      (a) Penalty. A contractual provision that fixes the consequences of a breach is
      enforceable as liquidated damages only if the harm is incapable or difficult of
      accurate estimation at the time of contracting and the stipulated amount is a
      reasonable forecast of that harm rather than a punishment. See Restatement
      (Second) of Contracts § 356(1). If the stipulated consequence is grossly
      disproportionate to the actual or anticipated loss, it is a penalty and is
      unenforceable. Connecticut courts have long applied this framework, and the
      difference between the amount at stake ($317 million at 90% completion, plus
      $5.7 million of posted security) and the Authority's actual loss from a delay
      (approximately $2.85 million per year of base rent) is the kind of disparity that has
      supported penalty findings.
      (b) Forfeiture. Separately, a court may excuse the non-occurrence of a condition
      — including a condition subsequent such as a reverter — where its enforcement
      would cause a disproportionate forfeiture, unless the condition was a material
      part of the agreed exchange. See Restatement (Second) of Contracts §§ 227(1),
      229. The rule of interpretation in § 227(1) counsels in favor of an interpretation
      that avoids forfeiture where the language is fairly susceptible of it. This doctrine
      is the more powerful of the two here, because it does not require us to
      characterize the reverter as a damages clause; it operates on the condition itself.
      (c) Unjust enrichment and constitutional limits. A public body that retains
      $300 million of privately financed improvements for a delay of months has been
      enriched without an corresponding legal basis, which is the classic predicate for
      restitution. Where the enriched party is a public body acting under color of a
      lease, there is also a colorable argument under Article First, § 11 of the
      Connecticut Constitution (private property shall not be taken for public use
      without just compensation) and Article First, § 1 (due process). We regard these
      as supplementary arguments, not the primary line: they are slower, less certain,
      and — critically — they are available only after the loss has occurred.




Hargrove & Linden LLP — Privileged and Confidential — Attorney Work Product                   Page 20 of 35
 6.2 What the client asked us to confirm
You asked us to confirm whether Connecticut law provides relief against a
disproportionate forfeiture, and referred to a prior matter "I think it was the Stamford
project" involving a principle "disfavoring penalties that are grossly disproportionate to
the actual harm suffered." We can confirm the principle: it is the mainstream American
rule, Connecticut applies it, and it is reflected in the Restatement sections cited above.
We cannot confirm the specific recollection. There is nothing in the record that
identifies a Stamford decision, and we are not able to verify a citation to one from the
documents in the file. We recommend a focused case-law search — specifically for
Connecticut ground lease, reverter, and commercial forfeiture decisions — before the
principle is invoked in negotiation with Pryor Whitfield & Koss, because the Authority's
counsel will ask for the cite and an incorrect one would cost credibility at the moment
we need it most.

6.3 The practical conclusion
The legal argument is sound but it should not be the strategy. An unenforceable clause
is a remedy you reach after two years of litigation, during which the improvements sit
in place, the construction loan is in default, and the equity is frozen. Bayside will not
underwrite the reverter on the theory that a court will rescue it; it will underwrite the
clause as written, or it will not close. The clause must therefore be fixed in the
document, and the legal analysis should be used for two narrower purposes: to give us
a credible fallback if the Authority refuses to move (we can say, in substance, that the
clause as drafted is unlikely to be enforced and that the Authority should prefer a
remedy it can actually obtain), and to support a savings and reformation provision in
the Lease itself (Section 9.10), which converts the argument into a drafting
mechanism.

6.4 Non-waivable rights and the savings clause
Section 9.10 and Section 16.10 of the draft are deliberate. They preserve Tenant's
right to seek relief from forfeiture, and they provide that if any provision is held to
operate as an unenforceable penalty the Lease shall be reformed to give effect to the
parties' intent — that Tenant be paid for the Improvements and that the Authority
recover only its actual, documented damages. A savings clause does two things: it
improves the odds of reformation rather than invalidation, and it gives the Lender
comfort that the remedy will not simply fail (leaving the Lender with a void termination
and an unclear estate).

                                      VII. ISSUE REGISTER

III. THE SIX CRITICAL ISSUES

A. The Reverter Right (Item 1)
1. What the Term Sheet does
Section 9 provides that if Tenant fails to achieve Milestone 1 (commencement of
construction by April 1, 2027) or Milestone 3 (substantial completion of Phase 1 by
October 1, 2030), the Authority may deliver a notice specifying the failure; Tenant then
has 180 days to cure; and if it does not, "the Lease shall automatically terminate upon
the expiration of such period," whereupon (a) Tenant forfeits the $5,700,000 letter of
credit, which the Authority "shall be entitled to draw in full," and (b) "[a]ll
improvements, structures, and fixtures constructed, installed, or placed on the
Premises by Tenant... shall immediately revert to and become the sole property of the




Hargrove & Linden LLP — Privileged and Confidential — Attorney Work Product   Page 4 of 34
 Landlord, free and clear of any claims by Tenant, without any payment, compensation,
or reimbursement to Tenant."
2. Why it fails as a matter of economics
The disproportionality is not marginal; it is roughly two orders of magnitude. Total
hard construction cost is $352,000,000 (Loan Term Sheet Section 3). At Milestone 3,
on a sixty-month schedule, the overwhelming majority of hard cost will already be in
the ground. If the milestone is missed at 90% completion, the value transferred to the
Authority is on the order of $317,000,000. The Authority's actual loss from a twelve-
month delay is the ground rent it did not receive during the delay — approximately
$2,850,000 — plus the loss of percentage rent, which at the projected breakpoint may
be nil, and which in any event is already captured because Base Rent does not begin
until the Rent Commencement Date. A remedy of $317,000,000 for a loss of
$2,850,000 is a ratio of roughly 111:1. Add the $5,700,000 letter of credit, which is
forfeited in addition, and the ratio exceeds 113:1.
The comparison to the Authority's actual damages is not merely an argument we would
make after the fact. It is the test a court would apply, and it is the test that matters for
negotiation, because a lender will not underwrite a collateral package whose value
turns on a clause that a court might or might not reform after eighteen months of
litigation.
3. What the Term Sheet already gives away
Two features of Section 9 make the position worse than it appears on first reading.
First, the reverter is triggered by a delay "even if Meridian is 95% complete," as you
put it, because there is no completion threshold, no materiality qualifier, and no
requirement that Tenant have abandoned the project. Second, the trigger is objective:
a missed date, not a failure to perform. A permitting holdup at the Building
Department, a supply-chain interruption in curtain wall, or a DEEP objection to the
ELUR would all produce a missed date without any fault on Meridian's part.
4. Our position
We have drafted Article 9 to preserve a reverter in form, because the Authority's Board
has resolved that the Lease include "reverter rights in favor of the Authority"
(Resolution No. 2025-047, Section 2(a)) and because we do not think the Authority will
abandon the concept at the first draft. But we have surrounded it with six conditions
precedent, each of which independently defeats it: (a) the improvements cannot vest in
the Authority unless and until the Authority pays a Purchase Price; (b) the Purchase
Price is the greater of the appraised Fair Market Value of the Improvements and
Tenant's Unreimbursed Hard Costs, net only of insurance, Landlord's documented
damages, and third-party recoveries; (c) Tenant may elect the Fair Market Value
measure and extinguish any Landlord damages claim; (d) if the Authority does not pay,
the termination is void, the Lease continues, and the Milestone is deemed satisfied; (e)
there is no forfeiture of the security deposit, which is limited to actual documented
loss; and (f) the reverter is unavailable altogether if the work is 90% or more complete
(measured by hard costs), in which case the Authority's remedies are specific
performance and damages only.
Separately, we have deleted the "automatic termination" language. Automatic
termination is not merely harsh; it is structurally incompatible with the lender
protections the same section purports to grant, because a lease that terminates by
operation of its own terms cannot be cured, and because the New Lease right depends
on there being an identifiable termination event and a notice to the Lender.

 5. Conditions to the reverter that are not currently in the Term Sheet
